Written Testimony in Support of LD 1705 An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding & Oversight Submitted by: Aimee Morrison College & Career Success Coordinator (WCCC) Maine Jobs Recovery Plan (MJRP) April 30th, 2025
Dear House of Representatives,
I am writing in strong support of bill LD1705, which provides emergency funding to ensure the continued employment of the College & Career Success Coordinators (CCSC) in adult education programs and community colleges across our state.
As a College & Career Success Coordinator, I have seen firsthand the transformative impact these positions have on the lives of adult learners. These positions are vital in bridging the gap between adult education and meaningful employment or postsecondary success. These coordinators provide individualized guidance, help navigate complex college and financial aid systems, support job readiness, and connect students with training opportunities that align with local workforce needs.
In rural communities, one of the greatest barriers our learners face is reliable transportation. Many adult learners live far from testing centers or community colleges, making it extremely difficult to access essential services like HiSET testing, college advising, or workforce training. With the flexibility and dedication of our positions coupled with the collaboration of adult education programs, I can extend proctoring services for HiSET examination directly on campus. Students are no longer challenged with overcoming transportation barriers by having a more centralized location for HiSET tutoring and testing. The innovation solution dramatically improved the access and success rates for our rural learners in obtaining their high school equivalency diplomas.
Adult learners often face multiple barriers - such as childcare responsibilities, inconsistent work schedules, and limited digital literacy - that make the transition to college or career pathways more difficult. These coordinators offer tailored and consistent support that empowers students to stay on track and complete their educational and career goals.
If the WCCC CCSC position is not sustained through emergency funding, responsibility for HiSET services will shift back entirely to the adult education program. With only one remaining certified proctor in the county, it would be difficult to offer the same flexibility or accommodate the diverse scheduling needs of our learners. Limited staffing will mean fewer testing sessions, longer wait times, and reduced access for those juggling work and family responsibilities - ultimately putting students' progress on hold.
Without emergency funding, many of these positions are at risk. The loss would not only destabilize programs but would also jeopardize the progress of thousands of adult learners who

depend on these services. Investing in these college and career success coordinators is an investment in economic mobility, workforce development, and community resilience.
I urge you to vote in favor of this bill and help protect the vital support system that the College & Career Success Coordinators provide. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Aimee Morrison 207-214-7666 amorrison@mainecc.edu

TO: Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy
Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
FROM: Cait Gant Eliot, ME RE: Testimony in support of LD 1705, An Act regarding Adult Education Funding & Oversight
DATE: April 30, 2025
Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Cait Grant, and I live in Eliot, ME. I am also the Vice President of Economic & Educational Development at York County Community College (YCCC). I am writing today as a private citizen who cares deeply about Maine's adult learners to express strong support for LD1705, specifically the Career Advancement and Navigation Program. It is important to note that, although my professional life absolutely informs my testimony, I am not speaking on behalf of the Maine Community College System or York County Community College.
In York County 4.3% of our adult population does not have a high school diploma or equivalent, which is roughly 4,900 individuals. Across the state, the number increases to 4.9% and roughly 35,000 adults who do not have a high school diploma or equivalent. As our state looks to support our existing employers and attract new businesses to Maine, our role in educating our Maine residents becomes critical.
York County Community College's mission is to create an educated and skilled workforce for the State of Maine. One of the ways YCCC has done that is through developing relationships with local educational partners. I have seen the Career Advancement and Navigation Program deepen our connections with our York County Adult Education Centers and to create more meaningful, supported pathways for our adult learners as they make the transition from adult education into our short-term training, and certificate and degree programs. This initiative emphasizes the importance of academic support, success coaching, and individualized planning to promote self-sufficiency and career growth, all of which are necessary for our adult students to advance in their careers.
At York County Community College, we have a dedicated position to facilitate access and create pathways for adult students pursuing their high school diploma or working on their HiSET. This position is embedded at YCCC and collaborates closely with our local Career Center, providing essential resources for career planning and resume building. Our navigator

has also made strides in supporting multilingual learners, ensuring they have the necessary resources to complete their college coursework. YCCC's adult learners are not just students. They are often parents, caretakers, and are working to support their families. YCCC's learners are sometimes one flat tire, one sick parent, or one closed daycare away from stopping out of their programs. The navigator assists students in connecting with various community resources, including those provided by York County Community Action, the HOPE Scholarship Program, local food pantries, and Goodwill Workforce Solutions. While we cannot remove the barriers entirely, the Navigator can support students in accessing the resources they need to get one step closer to their educational and career goals.
In closing, I urge the committee to support the funding for this vital program. Investing in adult education programs like the Career Advancement and Navigation Program not only transforms lives but also strengthens our workforce and community. Together, we can build a brighter future for all residents of Maine.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Cait Grant, Eliot, ME 207-216-4477

I have had the privilege of working closely with a College and Career Support Coordinator through the Adult Education department of a local public-school district. The CCSC acts as a liaison and support to Adult Education students who are interested in furthering their education at one of the Maine Community Colleges.
I've seen firsthand how supportive she is and the positive difference it makes for many learners of a variety of ages, and many who are multi-language learners.
Oftentimes students returning to school after a period, students completing their high school education, or students for whom English is not the native language, don't have confidence in their abilities. Unfortunately, many of them haven't had positive experiences with school in the past. For these students, taking the next step to consider furthering their education at the college level can seem like a daunting endeavor.
I've witnessed the CCS Coordinator support many students through their uncertainty, apprehension and even fear by meeting them "where they are" and walking them through the steps, giving them practical experience, allowing their obstacles to dissipate.
The coordinator is friendly and kind and puts people at ease quickly as she is a good listener and understanding of students' feelings. She goes out to the surrounding Adult Ed programs regularly to introduce herself and is available to meet people to answer questions and assist them with applying for acceptance to the college. She also has organized several open house events where she gives tours of the campus and has several staff members of the college introduce themselves and offer information about different programs and services available to students.
The coordinator also meets with many students to offer academic support and assistance with building skills necessary to be a successful college student. She teaches skills like time management and organization, as well as study skills. These are all important aspects of learning. She is especially well-versed in teaching adult learners specifically and presenting information in a variety of ways.
The person with whom I've been fortunate to work offers positive energy and valuable experience to several committees on campus and contributes to the overall campus community in a meaningful way. My experience of the CCSC position is like that of a "Goodwill Ambassador for Education". She and the CCSC position are invaluable and impactful for many students at the college.
I highly encourage supporting LD 1705, An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight.

Testimony of Dollene Bailey My name is Dollene Bailey, and I am a proud mother, grandmother, and current college
student. Ever since I was a little girl growing up in Guyana, I dreamed of becoming a nurse. But coming from a poor family, college wasn't an option. After immigrating to the United States in May 2000, I worked hard to build a life. I went back to school while working full time and caring for my grandmother with Alzheimer's.
In 2007, I lost both my career and my home during the market crash. Though I kept going for the sake of my children, the weight of working, caregiving, and trying to go back to college made it impossible to pursue my degree. I only had time for certificates that helped temporarily.
Since moving to Maine, I've been given a second chance. My two oldest children now have families of their own, and my youngest just started college, with the support of the same program I'm in. This program has been life-changing. It guides us through financial aid, helps us navigate classes, and supports us through career transitions; mine from CNA to RN.
Returning to college in my fifties was intimidating, especially being in classrooms with students the age of my children. But the Adult Education staff have created a space where I feel welcomed, supported, and connected. The tutoring and academic help have made a world of difference especially since I had taken some of these classes before but needed help remembering key details.
This program is not just about getting a degree it's about rebuilding a dream I had to put on hold decades ago. That's why it's so important to continue funding College and Career Success positions. They are not just staff, they are lifelines for adult learners like me who are trying to build a better future, not only for myself but my family.

Dollene Bailey Adult Ed LD 1705

Testimony in Support of Legislative Document No. 1705, An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight
To the Honorable Members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Ersula Steward and I am an adult learner residing in Jay, Maine. I am writing today to wholeheartedly support Legislative Document No. 1705, "An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight," because I have personally experienced the transformative power of adult education in our state.
After being a stay-at-home mother for twelve years with a GED under my belt, the prospect of college at age 36 felt overwhelming. However, my experience at RSU 73 Spruce Mountain Adult Education, specifically through their college transitions program, changed the trajectory of my life. The dedicated teachers, Betsy and Michelle, created a supportive and encouraging environment where I began to recognize my own potential and rediscovered a genuine love for learning. They instilled in me the confidence to pursue my goals, something I hadn't felt possible before.
The college transitions program equipped me with the skills and knowledge necessary to successfully apply and begin classes at Central Maine Community College. While I am still on my journey to completing my degree, the skills I gained through adult education have already had a significant impact on my life. I am currently working fulltime, earning more money than I ever have, utilizing skills that have honed my knowledge and expertise.
My support for adult education extends beyond my personal success. I am now passionate about sharing my love for design and demonstrating that a non-traditional educational path is not only acceptable but can open up a world of possibilities. I had the privilege of speaking at the 2024 Maine Adult Education Association (MEAE) conference and recently returned from the 2025 Coalition on Adult Basic Education (COABE) National Conference, where I spoke about the critical importance of investing in marketing to reach more adult learners.
I firmly believe that by empowering adults, whether they are parents or not, we can create a ripple effect that enhances the next generation. If we invest in teaching and uplifting adults, we are directly contributing to a stronger future for our children and our communities.
This proposed funding is absolutely critical for individuals like myself - people who, for various reasons, have experienced a disruption in the "traditional pathway" of education. We are eager to learn, to improve our lives, and to contribute more meaningfully to our state. Adult education provides the essential support, encouragement, teaching, and opportunities that allow us to reach our full potential. Education, in all its forms, is paramount, and adult education serves a vital and often overlooked segment of our population.

Testimony of Rep. Holly T. Sargent introducing
LD 1705, An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
Honorable members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, I am Holly
Sargent, and I represent House District 147, which is the town of York. I am here today to present LD
1705, An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight.
As we all know, Adult Education plays a critical role in the State's workforce development strategy.
Maine's current landscape consists of over 65 Adult Education programs, which provide a range of
instructional services to help adults develop the skills for further educational opportunities, job training,
better employment, and to realize their full potential as productive workers, family members and
citizens.
Between July 1, 2023, and June 30, 2024, over 12,900 adult learners participated in Maine Adult Education programming in one or more of the following areas: High School Completion, English Language Acquisition, Foundational Math, College Transitions and Workforce Training and Development. Additionally, 972 Adult Education students earned a high school credential, and adult leamers earned over 2,600 certifications and credentials of value in high demand career fields.
Maine Adult Education is a vital resource for multilingual learners throughout Maine. In 2023-2024,
Adult Education programs served 6,365 multilingual learners, accounting for nearly 50% of students
served. These numbers have been growing in recent years, as more multilingual learners tum to Adult
Education for critical language services.
The goal for LD 1705 is to bolster Maine's Adult Education programs and support them in a manner
commensurate with the important role they play in our economy. This bill takes a crucial step by directing the Legislature to fully fund Adult Education programs according to the funding formula that has been in statute since 2007. During the time that this funding formula has been on the books, the Legislature has never appropriated adequate funding to fully meet the statutory funding obligation. The first step in ensuring our Adult Education programs can be successful in educating and training our workers is to fully fund the programs according to the statutory formula.

In 2023, this committee passed a bill that included a modest funding increase for Adult Education, and also established a working group at the Department of Education (DOE) to examine the Adult Education
subsidy formula (LD 258 -- Public Law 2023 Chapter 4l2; Part RRR, Sec. RRR-2). DOE convened this
working group, and it met seven times between April and June of 2024. The group determined that the way the current funding formula is implemented is neither fair nor meets the needs of all Adult
Education programs in the State. Despite the modest funding increase for Adult Education that we passed in 2023, given current appropriations, Adult Ed programs are only receiving 59% of the funding
they qualify for in the current statutory formula. Given the critical work Adult Education programs do,
we should strive to bring this number up to 100%.
LD 1705 also seeks to shore up our Adult Education programs by putting into statute the Career
Advancement and Navigation Program, which provides students at Maine's Community Colleges with academic support, advisory services, and referrals to community services. This program was initially established using American Rescue Plan funds and it has proven to be very successful during its two
years of operation.
Lastly, this bill also requires the Department of Education to annually assess adult education needs in the State and submit a report to the Legislature detailing its assessment and recommendations.
I want to highlight a few key functions of Adult Education in Maine that make it so critical to our state's
workforce development strategy. Adult Education programs provide:
Q Workforce development training that prepares students for in-demand jobs. 0 Adult basic education programs that help students gain the skills they need to succeed in the
workforce. 0 English language acquisition programs that support our state's growing immigrant and refugee
populations.
0 High school equivalency and diploma programs that provide a second chance for students who
didn't complete high school. 0 College transitions programming that helps students navigate the college application process and
succeed in higher education.
These programs are essential to building a strong and skilled workforce in Maine, and it's critical that we
provide the necessary funding and oversight to ensure their success.
Adult Education is more than just an education program - it's a lifeline for many Mainers who are
looking to improve their skills, gain employment and support their families. It's a key component of our
state's economic development strategy, and it's essential that we provide the necessary funding and
oversight to ensure its success.
I urge you to support LD 1705 and provide the necessary funding and oversight to ensure the success of
Adult Education in Maine. Thank you.

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Education and
Cultural Affairs Committee:
LD 1705, An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight (EMERGENCYL would establish the Career Advancement and Navigation Program within the Maine Department of Education (DOE), in collaboration with the Maine Community College System (MCCS). Furthermore, LD 1705 would establish annual reporting requirements for the DOE to the
Legislature regarding adult education programming and funding, establish significant oversight
duties for the DOE over adult education funding, and to convene a stakeholder group on a
biennial basis to provide input on statewide goals for adult education, funding priorities, and programmatic improvements.
Currently the DOE Adult Education Team plays a central role in overseeing, funding, and guiding
adult education programs across the state. It is responsible for determining and allocating funding levels, setting statewide goals, and ensuring program oversight and accountability.
Each year by February 1, the DOE notifies school administrative units (SAUs) of the estimated
subsidy funding they can expect for adult education programming in the upcoming fiscal year. These estimates are then included in the DOE's annual budget request to the Maine Legislature.
Subsidy funding is provided through reimbursement for eligible local expenses, specifically 75% for instruction, 70% for administration, and 50% for supplies--as long as these costs are
supported by local funds and tied directly to academic programming.
In addition to managing funding, the DOE Adult Education Team also sets goals and priorities
for adult education that align with the Workforce, innovation, and Opportunity Act (WIOA) and pertain to workforce development, high school equivalency attainment, English language learning, and lifelong education. Adult education priorities are also informed by communication with the field- through regular meetings with directors, case management, and advisory committees. The Department supports statewide initiatives to improve literacy, career
readiness, and professional development for adult educators. The Adult Education Team

recommendations or adjustments as needed. Through these efforts, the Maine DOE ensures
that adult education remains accessible, effective, and aligned with the state's broader educational and economic objectives.
The DOE also manages data systems and requires adult education units to submit detailed,
timely reports as part of their subsidy funding eligibility process. Non-compliance with
information requests may result in the withholding of subsidy payments. The DOE oversees the
EF-X-132 subsidy form process, which must be completed annually by September 15, using data from the prior academic year.
While Section 5 of LD 1705, which ensures 100% state funding of adult education obligations,
aims to strengthen Maine's adult education system, it also brings several potential impacts
particularly for the DOE and the broader education and budgetary landscape.
The College and Career Success Coordinator positions are a Maine Jobs and Recovery Plan
funded project that have had great success in serving new and perspective community college
students making the transition to post-secondary education. Over 3,000 participants have benefited from this extra support offered on campus. These funds are expiring in 2026. These positions play an important role in the workforce and educational landscape of Maine, one that won't truly be felt until the positions are eliminated. The requirement to employ a College and
Career Success Coordinator at each community college campus would mean the DOE must recruit, hire, and manage multiple new staff members statewide and coordinate closely with the Maine Community College System to align goals and services, and oversee program
implementation and on-site support services, expanding beyond its traditional oversight role into direct service delivery. This represents a significant expansion of operational scope and
resource commitment and deserves its own funding allocation.
Additionally, guaranteeing 100% of the funding obligation could strain the General Fund, especially during economic downturns. Knowing that the State is covering all obligated costs might also discourage local districts from investing additional funds into adult education. The increased state role and strict reimbursement criteria could standardize programs in a way that limits local flexibility. Communities may find it harder to adapt programs to local needs if
funding is tightly controlled or if the DOE's administrative processes are rigid or slow to adapt. Implementing a full-scale funding change and the infrastructure to support it could be logistically difficult, especially if timelines are aggressive.
While the appropriation is mandated by statute, it still depends on the Legislature's budget approval process. Political or economic changes could lead to underfunding or repeal, creating uncertainty and undermining program planning at the local level.

Testimony to support LD 1705 - An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight
April 30, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs,
My name is Shirley Wright, and l am the Executive Director of the Maine Adult Education
Association (MAEA), a professional nonprofit organization that supports adult education programs across the state through advocacy, professional development, and collaboration.
l am writing to express MAEA's strong support for LD 1705, submitted by Representative Holly
Sargent, which seeks to accomplish two critical and long-overdue actions for the benefit of Maine's adult leamers.
1. Support for College and Career Success Coordinators
First, this bill requests state funding for the College and Career Success Coordinators
(CCSCs)--a group of dedicated professionals who are hired by local adult education programs but based at each of Maine's seven community college campuses. These coordinators are the
vital bridge between adult learners and successful postsecondary transition.
Their work is making a difference. CCSCs provide personalized support that helps adults build
academic confidence, navigate enrollment and financial aid systems, and persist through the
first critical year of college. Many of these learners are first-generation college students, working
adults, parents, or returning learners with unique challenges. CCSCs meet them where they are
and walk alongside them through this transition.
This Maine Jobs and Recovery Plan model is working, and we can provide data to show increased college enrollment and persistence among adult learners who receive this support.
However, the program's future is uncertain without an additional $338,000 of sustainable state
funding through June of 2026. LD 1705 recognizes the value of this investment and asks the
state to commit to it in the future.

2. Full Funding for Adult Education Subsidy
The second component of this bill is equally urgent. For more than a decade, the state has calculated the adult education subsidy based on an expenditure model that aligns with current law. And yet, year after year, programs receive only half--or, in many cases, less than that of the amount that is due to them. This persistent underfunding occurs not because of changes in need or formula, but because the state fails to allocate enough funds to meet its own obligations. Furthermore, the state's subsidy notification letter that goes to school superintendents fails to mention the amount due to each program compared to the actual amount to be received and the prorate or reduction is never mentioned.
The results are serious. Adult education programs employ part-time staff, experience high turnover rates among experienced staff, and are unable to expand sen/ices at a time when the state needs them more than ever. Whether it's helping adults complete high school, learn English, gain digital skills, or train for careers, adult education is a cornerstone of Maine's workforce and career development system. Programs should not be penalized for doing more with less year after year. The local share for each adult education program far outweighs the
state share.
It is time for Maine to fully fund the adult education subsidy at the level prescribed by law and
the level adult learners deserve.
ln closing, LD 1705 addresses two of the most critical gaps in Maine's adult education landscape. It is a fonlvard-thinking, cost-effective way to strengthen our workforce, support
families, and ensure that all Maine adults have the opportunity to succeed.
On behalf of the Maine Adult Education Association, l urge you to support this bill and provide the funding and support that our learners and programs need to thrive. l am attaching data to
support our request for this testimony.
Thank you for your time and for your commitment to adult education.
Respectfully submitted,
Shirley `N. `Wright
Shirley Wright, Executive Director, Maine Adult Education Association

Testimony to support LD 1705 - An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight
April 30, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs
My name is Stephanie Haskins, and I am the Director of Gray-New Gloucester Adult Education. I have served those communities for 11 years in this capacity. In addition, I have served as the coleader for the College and Career Success Coordinator position at Southern Maine Community College since its inception.
I am writing to express my strong support for LD 1705, "An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight", submitted by Representative Holly Sargent, which addresses several critical needs within Maine's adult education system. I enthusiastically support the request that Maine fully fund the adult education subsidy at the level prescribed by law as well as the College and Career Success Coordinator positions at Maine Community Colleges.
Adult Education programs across the state play a vital role in helping Maine reach economic goals. Adult Learners can access academic, college and career supports, which include basic skills (reading, writing, math, digital literacy, English language acquisition) to pursue their career goals. While funding continues to stream to Community Colleges, it is important to note the vital role Adult Education plays in preparing adults for the rigors of community college. Adult Education is often the first step for many learners who don't have the skills and or confidence to enter community college or a training program.
Maine Adult Education programs are highly accessible, with more than 70 locations across the state, and provide the basic skills learners need to obtain a credential of value and help our state develop a skilled workforce. Local districts contribute significantly to adult education programs in the form of local tax dollars and space to operate. It is time our state recognizes the value these programs add to achieving our economic goals. My small program alone has awarded more than 170 Certified Clinical Medical Assistant Certifications and more than 50 Maine State Certified Nursing Assistant credentials since August of 2020. These learners have all increased their employability, are now earning a livable wage, and many have continued to further their education. Additional funding would allow my program to better serve learners by increasing our instructional availability and attracting and retaining high quality educators. Meeting funding obligations to Adult Education directly impacts our state economy by helping build a skilled workforce.
Additionally, this bill asks for state funding for the College and Career Success Coordinators (CCSCs)--a group of dedicated professionals hired by local adult education programs but based at each of Maine's seven community college campuses. These coordinators are the vital bridge between adult learners and successful postsecondary transition.

Local data from College Success Coordinator reporting has unequivocally shown that having an Adult Education contact on campus at SMCC has been of tremendous benefit. Compiling data from FY24 of the SMCC Maine Jobs and Recovery Act Success Coordinator showed 477 students were served. Of those 477 students served, 167 were referred from adult education to the success coordinator, 107 were referred to their local adult education programs to build the necessary skills to succeed, 122 were enrolled in SMCC as new students, 131 took one or more free adult education classes to develop skills and 30 were co-enrolled at SMCC while receiving adult education services.
Making referrals to partner programs to help reduce barriers to success is a significant part of the success coordinator's role. During FY24, 388 referrals were made to outside agencies to help support student success. The most notable referrals were 79 to the Scholarship for Maine Immigrants, 84 to the Maine Community Foundation, 57 to the Wildflower Foundation, and 45 to the Maine Educational Opportunity Center. Other notable agencies receiving referrals were TRIO, MCCA, USM, CLEP, UMaine, SMCC Social Work (Housing), and others. Connecting students to resources is invaluable in reducing barriers and helping them achieve their academic and career goals.
The demographics of students served by the College Success Coordinator also highlight the success of this program in helping those who are Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed, and new Mainers, as well as other historically marginalized populations. While the data collected doesn't explicitly detail some of those categories, it does provide a glimpse of the students served. Of students with completed intakes during FY24, 92.1% were from low- to middle-income backgrounds; 29.6% reported being unemployed, and 42.7% reported being underemployed. Additionally, 71.1% of the learners were multilingual, and 67.9% were Black, Indigenous People of Color (BIPOC).
The benefit of having an Adult Education representative located on Community College campus is apparent in the data. While this data represents one year of the program, it has been consistent since implementation. Not only have learners from Adult Education benefited from this liaison, but also learners seeking community college, who aren't ready for the rigor, have also benefited from referrals back to Adult Education. Continuation of this program in its full-time status will provide a significant benefit to learners seeking to increase their employability and academic skills.
In conclusion, I urge you to support LD 1705 to provide necessary funding to often overlooked learners in our state; learners who are poised to positively impact the economic growth of our state. This bill will strengthen adult education in Maine, empower our residents, and contribute to the economic and social well-being of our state.
Thank you for your time and commitment to Adult Education.
Respectfully,
Stephanie Haskins, Director, Gray-New Gloucester Adult Education

Thank you for allowing me to submit written testimony. I am an adult education director who works closely with the Maine College and Career Success Coordinators placed at our 7 Community Colleges. In Maine, our locations are either at a public school or other town location but not on a college campus. When the MJRP coordinators were established at each college, our job and outreach became so much easier. Prior to these positions being created it took much longer to navigate the ever changing College system and staff. To have someone on site, with current information and contacts on campus gives us the best of both worlds, our adult education service in our local district AND at the Community Colleges in Maine. Students can come to our location or we can go to the campus to work with them. I have done both in my time as an adult educator. I hope my small testimony makes a difference in enabling these positions to continue.

Testimony to support LD 1705 - An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and Oversight
April 30, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs,
My name is Thomas Nash, and l have been the Director of Windham Raymond Adult Education (WRAE) in the RSU #14 School District for over 21 years. l have also proudly served as an adult education administrator in three
other districts, totaling almost 40 years of helping to improve the lives of adult learners through education.
I am here today to express my strong support for LD 1705, "An Act Regarding Adult Education Funding and
Oversight" , submitted by Representative Holly Sargent, which addresses several critical needs within Maine's adult education system. The passage of this bill would represent a significant step forward in strengthening educational opportunities for Maine residents.
Firstly, LD 1705 codifies the Career Advancement and Navigation Program, requesting funding for the College
and Career Success Coordinators (CCSCs), which has proven to be highly successful. This program provides invaluable personalized support to students, including academic guidance, transition assistance for those entering
community college, and referrals to essential resources. By ensuring the continuation of this program, we are
investing in the success of our students, their families, and, ultimately, in the success of our workforce. At
Southern Maine Community College, where our regional CCSC is based, over the past six months alone, 158
contacts have occurred, resulting in 41 academic and career plans created for students, 125 referrals to outside
partner agencies, 37 new community college enrollees, and 53 interagency contacts.
Secondly, this bill takes necessary steps towards improving the funding and oversight of adult education programs across the state. lt mandates annual assessments of adult education needs, requires detailed reporting on funding and outcomes, and establishes clear guidelines for the use of state funds. These measures will promote transparency, accountability, and efficiency in the allocation of resources, ultimately benefiting both programs and our adult students.
Finally, LD 1705 acknowledges the chronic underfunding of adult education and takes steps to address it. By requiring the Legislature to appropriate 100% of the state's obligation for adult education funding, this bill
underscores the importance of these programs. lt ensures they receive` the necessary financial support to fulfill
their vital mission. For example, over the past five years, WRAE received local tax contributions of $1,575,682 and state adult education subsidies of $801,716. A 100% state obligation would have resulted in an additional
$782,807 for our program. That would have allowed us to employ and retain full-time teaching staff and expand our services at a time when the state needed well-educated, well-trained adults to enter our workforce or reskill.
ln conclusion, on behalf of the adult learners in my program, in my region, and throughout the state, l urge you to support LD 1705 and provide the necessary funding and assistance that our learners and programs deserve. This bill will strengthen adult education in Maine, empower our residents, and contribute to the economic and social
well-being of our state.
Thank you for your time and your commitment to adult education.
Respectfully submitted,

Thomas Nash, Director, indham Raymond Adult Education
